title: 1.3.21 Module 1.3 Quiz
description: Six multiple-choice questions on naming, variable reuse, and when a name beats a comment. Checked instantly.

questions.question: Why is `let a = 5;` a poor variable name?
options: Single letters are illegal in JavaScript
It says nothing about what the 5 is, so a reader has to work it out from the rest of the code
It makes the program run more slowly
Variable names must be at least three characters
questions.explanation: It is legal and it is fast — it is just silent. `let sideLength = 5;` tells the next reader what the 5 means without them having to reconstruct it.

questions.question: What is the problem with reusing one variable to hold different kinds of values?
options: JavaScript will refuse to run it
It uses more memory than separate variables
The name can only be true for one of them, so the code stops matching what it says
Nothing — it is good practice, because it keeps the program short
questions.explanation: A variable called `temp` that holds a temperature, then a name, then a total is lying two thirds of the time. Separate meanings want separate names.

questions.question: True or false: using extra variables slows your program down.
options: True — every variable costs measurable speed
False — the cost is far too small to matter, and clear names are worth much more
True — but only in the browser
False — extra variables actually make programs faster
questions.explanation: False. Naming an intermediate value costs essentially nothing at runtime and buys a lot of readability. Do not trade clarity for a saving you cannot measure.

questions.question: Which pair of names follows the "descriptive but concise" guideline?
options: x and num
data and abc
userName and totalPrice
theNameOfTheCurrentlyLoggedInUser and theGrandTotalOfAllItems
questions.explanation: userName and totalPrice say what they hold without becoming a sentence. x, num, data and abc say nothing; the last pair says it three times over.

questions.question: Which variable would sensibly hold a boolean?
options: let studentName
let itemCount
let isTaskFinished
let priceWithCents
questions.explanation: A boolean is true or false, so a yes/no name fits it — `isTaskFinished`. A name, a count and a price are a string and two numbers.

questions.question: Someone says "the comment above this line explains it, so the variable name does not matter." Why is a good name still better?
options: Comments are not allowed in professional code
The name travels with the variable everywhere it is used; the comment only sits in one place, and can drift out of date
Comments make the file too large
A good name makes the program run faster than a comment does
questions.explanation: You read the name at every use and the comment only once, at the declaration — and when the code changes, the comment is the part that quietly stops being true.
